title: Model Update and Rollback Lifecycle
summary: This intermediate module enables learners to plan a model update as a controlled release and decide when to continue, stop, or roll back. After completing it, learners can define an update baseline, acceptance evidence, rollout observations, and a compatible rollback unit.
objectives: Define the baseline, acceptance criteria, and evidence required before releasing a model update.
Plan a controlled rollout that compares observed results with predetermined acceptance criteria.
Identify when a rollback is appropriate and specify the complete compatible release unit that must be restored.
Create a release record that supports later investigation and review.

sections.title: What changed in this update
paragraphs: The previous citation, content/modules/self-hosted-model-operations/model-update-and-rollback-lifecycle.json, was an internal catalogue path attributed to an unregistered publisher and had never been verified. It is not retained as evidence.

That citation was replaced with public sources covering machine learning production risks, production-readiness testing, release engineering, and ongoing risk management. The correction affects the support for the module's guidance on testing before release, monitoring during release, and preparing a rollback. No provider-specific procedure, tool command, version number, or configuration key has been added.

sections.title: Level and scope
paragraphs: This is an intermediate-level module. It assumes that the learner already understands the basic meanings of a model, a validation dataset, a metric, and a production deployment. It does not assume experience with any particular provider or operational tool.

A model update is treated here as an operational change rather than as a model file in isolation. Machine learning systems can accumulate dependencies involving data, interfaces, and surrounding system behavior, so an update plan must account for the parts that need to remain compatible.

sections.title: Define the baseline and release unit
paragraphs: Begin by naming the baseline, which is the last accepted release against which the candidate update will be compared. A comparison is meaningful only when the team can identify what is being compared and which evidence will determine acceptance.

Define the release unit as the model artifact together with the coupled elements required for compatible operation. Depending on the system, those elements can include input and output expectations, preprocessing or postprocessing behavior, and required dependencies. Include an element only when changing or restoring the model without it could break compatibility.
The rollback target is the last accepted compatible release unit, not automatically the model artifact alone. Record how that unit can be identified and restored before beginning the rollout.

sections.title: Prepare acceptance evidence
paragraphs: Choose acceptance criteria before release. Criteria should cover the model behavior and operational behavior relevant to the system's stated requirements. Each criterion needs a defined observation, an acceptable result, and a decision that follows if the result is unacceptable.

Run the candidate and baseline through the same applicable checks so that the comparison is not changed by using different evaluation conditions. Production-readiness guidance for machine learning systems emphasizes testing data, model behavior, and serving behavior rather than relying on a single aggregate score.

Record the candidate identifier, baseline identifier, evaluation conditions, results, known limitations, decision, and responsible reviewer. This record connects the evidence available before release with the later decision to continue or roll back.

sections.title: Control and observe the release
paragraphs: Use a limited initial release when the operating environment supports one. The purpose is to restrict exposure while checking whether the candidate behaves as expected under production conditions. A limited release does not replace pre-release evaluation because it exposes real users or workloads to the candidate.

Observe the criteria selected before release. Continue only when the evidence satisfies those criteria. Stop expansion when the evidence is missing, ambiguous, or outside an accepted limit. Risk-management guidance treats post-deployment monitoring and documented response plans as continuing parts of system management.

Do not redefine an unacceptable result as acceptable merely because the rollout has started. If a criterion was poorly chosen, stop the decision process, document the issue, and conduct a new review rather than silently changing the rule.

sections.title: Roll back and verify recovery
paragraphs: A rollback restores the last accepted compatible release unit after the candidate fails an acceptance criterion or creates an unacceptable operational condition. The decision should use the predetermined criteria and response plan rather than an improvised judgment made after impact is visible.

Before release, verify that the rollback target is available and that the restoration procedure can be performed. Release-engineering guidance emphasizes repeatable processes and the ability to address release problems predictably.

After restoration, verify that the system is operating with the intended rollback unit and that the condition that triggered rollback is no longer present. Preserve the observations, decision, and recovery result for investigation. A successful restoration limits exposure, but it does not explain why the candidate failed.
sections.callout: Do not assume that restoring only a model artifact completes a rollback. Restore and verify the entire compatible release unit defined before rollout.

sections.title: Close the lifecycle
paragraphs: If the candidate is accepted, record the evidence and identify it as the new accepted baseline. If it is rolled back, retain the prior baseline and document the failed criteria, observed impact, restoration result, and required follow-up.

The lifecycle is complete only when the release decision and its evidence are recorded. This produces a traceable path from candidate evaluation to controlled release, observation, decision, and recovery.

questions.prompt: What should be defined before a candidate model begins its rollout?
choices: The baseline, compatible release unit, acceptance criteria, and rollback target
New acceptance criteria to be selected after production results appear
A provider-specific command and configuration key
questions.explanation: The module requires the team to define the baseline, complete compatible release unit, predetermined acceptance criteria, and rollback target before rollout.

questions.prompt: When should rollout expansion stop according to this module?
choices: Only after the entire rollout is complete
Whenever the candidate differs from the baseline in any way
When required evidence is missing, ambiguous, or outside an accepted limit
Only when the model artifact cannot be found
questions.explanation: The controlled-release section says to stop expansion when evidence is missing, ambiguous, or outside a predetermined accepted limit.

questions.prompt: What is the correct rollback target?
choices: The last accepted compatible release unit
The candidate with its acceptance criteria removed
questions.explanation: The rollback target is the last accepted compatible release unit, which can include the model and any coupled elements required for compatible operation.

questions.prompt: What source change prompted this correction?

A model benchmark was assigned a new score
